ipp_page_h1: Hospital Isolated Power Panels (IPP) — NFPA 99 Compliant Solutions Across Saudi Arabia
ipp_page_subhead: Life-critical power protection for operating rooms, ICUs & wet procedure locations
ipp_what_heading: What Is an Isolated Power Panel?
ipp_what_p1: An isolated power panel (IPP) is a hospital-grade electrical system required in operating rooms and other "wet procedure locations" under NFPA 99. Instead of grounding the electrical system directly, an IPP electrically isolates the power supply so that a single ground fault does not trip the breaker or interrupt power — critical equipment stays running while the fault is detected and alarmed.
ipp_what_p2: This matters because in an operating room, an unexpected power interruption during a procedure is not just inconvenient — it can be dangerous. A line isolation monitor (LIM) continuously watches for faults and alerts staff immediately, giving the surgical team time to respond safely without the system cutting power outright.
ipp_step1_desc: Equipment sourcing matched to your facility's requirements, with compliance verification against NFPA 99 before anything is ordered.
ipp_step2_desc: Site assessment, electrical integration with existing systems, and equipotential grounding setup carried out by our installation team.
ipp_step3_desc: Full functional testing of every circuit and alarm, line isolation monitor calibration, and documentation before handover.
ipp_step4_desc: Hands-on training for hospital personnel on system operation, alarm response, and maintenance protocols.
ipp_step5_desc: Scheduled preventive maintenance, system inspections, and emergency response support to keep your IPP system compliant and reliable.

ev_page_h1: EV Charging Station Installation Across Saudi Arabia — AC & DC Fast Chargers
ev_page_subhead: OCPP-compliant charging infrastructure for malls, hotels, offices, government facilities & fleets
ev_what_p1: EV charging infrastructure covers the equipment, electrical integration, and network software that lets electric vehicles recharge safely and efficiently at a fixed location. This ranges from AC Level 2 chargers suited to workplaces and residential compounds, to DC fast chargers built for high-throughput sites like malls, highway service stations, and fleet depots.
ev_what_p2: A properly installed charging station is more than a wall-mounted unit — it requires load calculation against the building's existing electrical capacity, correct circuit protection, and, for commercial sites, a network layer (OCPP) that handles payment, access control, and remote diagnostics across multiple chargers and locations.
ev_breakdown_heading: From Site Survey to Ongoing Network Support

ev_step2_desc: AC Level 2 and DC fast charger sourcing, sized and specified to your site's expected usage and vehicle mix.
ev_step3_desc: Electrical integration with existing infrastructure, circuit protection, and physical mounting carried out by our installation team.
ev_step4_desc: Full functional testing of every charge point, network connectivity verification, and payment/RFID system checks before handover.
ev_step5_desc: Scheduled preventive maintenance, firmware updates, and remote monitoring to keep chargers online and earning revenue.

ups_page_h1: UPS Systems & Power Backup Solutions Across Saudi Arabia
ups_page_subhead: Online double-conversion, line-interactive & standby UPS from 1kVA to 1MVA for zero-downtime operations
ups_what_p1: An Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) sits between the utility grid and your critical equipment, instantly switching to battery power the moment mains power fails or fluctuates outside safe limits. For mission-critical systems — servers, medical equipment, production lines, control rooms — even a fraction-of-a-second gap in power can mean lost data, halted processes, or equipment damage.
ups_what_p2: UPS systems range from small standby units protecting a single server rack to large online double-conversion systems supporting an entire data center or manufacturing floor. The right topology and capacity depend on your load profile, required runtime, and how much power quality protection your equipment needs beyond simple outage backup.
ups_breakdown_heading: From Load Assessment to Long-Term Support
ups_step1_desc: Detailed load analysis and runtime requirements to size the correct UPS capacity and battery bank for your facility.
ups_step2_desc: Sourcing of online double-conversion, line-interactive, or standby UPS systems matched to your operational requirements.
ups_step3_desc: Electrical integration, battery bank installation, and connection to existing distribution boards carried out by our team.
ups_step4_desc: Full load-bank testing, transfer-switch verification, and runtime confirmation before your systems go live.
ups_step5_desc: Scheduled battery testing, capacity assessments, and runtime optimization to catch degradation before it causes downtime.

hvac_page_h1: Commercial HVAC Installation & Maintenance Across Saudi Arabia
hvac_page_subhead: Air handling units, VRF/VRV systems & BMS-integrated smart controls for reliable climate control
hvac_what_p1: Commercial HVAC covers the equipment and controls that heat, cool, ventilate, and filter air across a building — central plant chillers, air handling units (AHUs), ductwork and diffusers, and the automation layer that ties it all together. Unlike residential systems, commercial HVAC has to handle variable occupancy, mixed-use zones, and often continuous operation.
hvac_what_p2: Correct sizing matters more than most building owners realize — an oversized system short-cycles and wastes energy, while an undersized one never keeps up on peak summer days. We size systems against real load calculations for your building, not rule-of-thumb estimates, and integrate controls so the system runs efficiently rather than just running.

hvac_step3_desc: Ductwork fabrication and installation, air balancing, and equipment mounting carried out by our installation team.
hvac_step4_desc: BMS integration, zone temperature setup, and full commissioning testing before handover.
hvac_step5_desc: Filter replacement, coil cleaning, refrigerant checks, and scheduled inspections to protect efficiency and equipment life.

fire_page_h1: Fire Detection & Suppression Systems Across Saudi Arabia
fire_page_subhead: Addressable fire alarm panels, sprinkler networks & suppression systems built for compliance and rapid response
fire_what_p1: A complete fire protection system combines detection (smoke, heat, and gas sensors tied to an addressable alarm panel), suppression (sprinklers, clean-agent systems, or water mist depending on the risk), and manual intervention equipment (hydrants, hose reels, extinguishers) — all designed to work together during an actual event, not just pass an inspection.
fire_what_p2: The right combination depends on occupancy type and fire risk: a server room needs clean-agent suppression that won't damage equipment, a warehouse needs sprinkler density matched to stored commodity class, and a high-rise needs standpipe and hose reel systems integrated with evacuation planning. We design to the actual risk, not a generic checklist.
fire_step1_desc: Occupancy and hazard analysis to determine the right detection and suppression system type for your facility.
fire_step2_desc: Sourcing of addressable panels, detectors, sprinkler components, and suppression agents matched to the design.
fire_step3_desc: Piping, wiring, panel installation, and integration with building evacuation and BMS systems.

elec_page_h1: Electrical & Power Distribution Systems Across Saudi Arabia
elec_page_subhead: Switchgear, distribution boards & control panels engineered for safe, reliable power delivery
elec_what_p1: Power distribution is the layer between the utility connection and every load in a building — main distribution boards (MDB), sub-distribution boards (SMDB), final distribution boards (DB), switchgear, and the control panels (MCC, PLC, SCADA) that automate and protect the system. Getting this layer right determines whether a facility runs reliably or suffers nuisance trips and downtime.
elec_what_p2: We design distribution systems around your actual load schedule and future expansion plans, not just present-day demand, and size protection devices, cabling, and containment (trays, conduits, busbars) to match — so the system has headroom rather than running at its limit from day one.

faq_q1: What areas of Saudi Arabia does Black Arrow serve?
faq_a1: We serve clients nationwide across Saudi Arabia, with our strongest coverage in Riyadh, Jeddah, Dammam, Al Khobar, and the Eastern Province. Site visits, installation, and maintenance are arranged based on your project location.
faq_q2: What industries does Black Arrow work with?
faq_a2: We work with hospitals and healthcare facilities, government facilities, commercial buildings (malls, offices, retail), industrial plants, hotels and hospitality, and aviation facilities — each with infrastructure solutions tailored to that sector's compliance and operational needs.
faq_q3: How do I request a quote?
faq_a3: You can request a quote through our contact page, by calling +966 560 224 715, or via WhatsApp. Include your project type and location so we can route your request to the right team.
faq_q4: Does Black Arrow only supply equipment, or do you also install and maintain it?
faq_a4: We handle the full lifecycle — supply, installation, testing/commissioning, and ongoing maintenance — for our core service lines (isolated power panels, EV charging, UPS, HVAC, lighting, firefighting, and electrical distribution).
faq_q5: What is an isolated power panel (IPP) and why do hospitals need one?
faq_a5: An isolated power panel is a hospital-grade electrical system required in operating rooms and other wet procedure locations under NFPA 99. It electrically isolates the power supply so a single ground fault doesn't interrupt power to life-critical equipment — a line isolation monitor alerts staff to the fault instead of cutting power outright.
faq_q6: Which IPP brands does Black Arrow supply?
faq_a6: We supply Bender isolated power panels (we are not an authorized or exclusive Bender dealer) and PG LifeLink IPP panels. Our designs are also compatible with Schneider Electric-style isolated power system specifications where a project calls for it.
faq_q7: What standards do your isolated power panels comply with?
faq_a7: Our IPP installations are engineered to NFPA 99, NFPA 70, and applicable SASO requirements for installed electrical equipment in Saudi Arabia.
faq_q8: What EV chargers does Black Arrow install?
faq_a8: We install AC Level 2 chargers (7–22kW) for workplaces and residential compounds, and DC fast chargers (50–350kW) for high-throughput commercial sites, with OCPP-compliant network management for multi-site operations and integrated POS/RFID payment where needed.
faq_q9: Can Black Arrow set up EV charging with a payment system?
faq_a9: Yes — we integrate POS, RFID card access, and mobile app payment options into commercial EV charging installations, along with OCPP-based remote monitoring and network management.
faq_q10: What size UPS system do I need?
faq_a10: It depends on your critical load and required runtime. We start with a load assessment to size the correct UPS capacity (we install systems from 1kVA up to 1MVA) and battery bank, rather than recommending a size before understanding your actual load profile.
faq_q11: What's the difference between online, line-interactive, and standby UPS?
faq_a11: Online (double-conversion) UPS continuously conditions power and offers the highest protection, suited to mission-critical loads. Line-interactive UPS regulates voltage and switches to battery on outage, a good middle-ground option. Standby UPS is the simplest and most economical, switching to battery only when mains power fails outright. We recommend the right topology based on your equipment's sensitivity and your budget.
faq_q12: Do you supply HVAC systems for both new buildings and retrofits?
faq_a12: Yes. We size systems based on a real load calculation for your building — whether it's new construction or a retrofit — rather than rule-of-thumb estimates, covering VRF/VRV systems, central chiller plants, and packaged rooftop units.
faq_q13: What fire suppression systems does Black Arrow install?
faq_a13: We install water sprinkler systems, clean-agent suppression (FM-200, CO₂), and water mist systems, matched to your facility's occupancy type and hazard classification, along with addressable fire alarm detection and hydrant/hose reel systems.
faq_q14: Are your fire safety systems compliant with Saudi civil defense requirements?
faq_a14: Yes, our fire detection and suppression designs follow NFPA 13 and NFPA 72 standards alongside Saudi Civil Defense requirements, with full testing and documentation provided for approval.
faq_q15: What electrical panel types does Black Arrow supply?
faq_a15: We supply and install main distribution boards (MDB), sub-distribution boards (SMDB), final distribution boards (DB), switchgear, and MCC/PLC/SCADA-integrated control panels for both low-voltage and medium-voltage systems.

nfpa_post_title: NFPA 99 Compliance for Saudi Hospitals: A Practical Guide
nfpa_post_excerpt: What NFPA 99 covers, why it matters for hospital electrical systems, and a practical compliance checklist for facility managers.
nfpa_post_h1: NFPA 99 Compliance for Saudi Hospitals: A Practical Guide
nfpa_post_subhead: What the standard covers, why it matters for electrical systems, and what to check before your next inspection
nfpa_p1: If you're involved in planning, building, or maintaining a hospital in Saudi Arabia, you've likely come across NFPA 99 — the "Health Care Facilities Code" published by the U.S. National Fire Protection Association. It isn't a Saudi legal requirement in the way SASO or Saudi Civil Defense codes are, but it's widely referenced by hospital accreditation bodies, international design consultants, and medical equipment manufacturers operating in the Kingdom, which makes it a de facto standard for anyone building or upgrading a modern healthcare facility here.
nfpa_p2: NFPA 99 is broad — it covers everything from medical gas systems to laboratory safety. For infrastructure and electrical contractors, the most relevant sections are the ones governing "essential electrical systems" (backup power for life-safety and critical branches) and "wet procedure locations" (operating rooms and similar spaces where conductive liquids and electrical equipment are both present).
nfpa_p3: The code classifies patient care spaces into categories based on the risk to patients if electrical power fails or a fault occurs — a general patient room has different requirements than an operating room, and getting that classification right at the design stage determines what equipment you actually need to install.
nfpa_h2_2: Why Wet Procedure Locations Get Special Treatment
nfpa_p4: In an operating room, a patient's body and surgical equipment can create a low-resistance path to ground through conductive fluids. A standard grounded electrical system will trip a breaker the moment a single fault occurs — which is exactly the wrong behavior when a surgical team is mid-procedure and depends on continuous power to monitors, ventilators, and surgical equipment.
nfpa_p5: This is why NFPA 99 requires an isolated power system for these spaces in most cases: it electrically isolates the circuit from ground so a single fault doesn't interrupt power, while a line isolation monitor immediately alerts staff to the fault so it can be corrected — usually between procedures, not during one.
nfpa_check_1: Confirm which NFPA 99 patient care category applies to each space in your facility — this drives every downstream electrical decision.
nfpa_check_2: Verify isolated power panels are installed and functioning in all wet procedure locations (ORs, and other areas your design consultant flags).
nfpa_check_3: Test line isolation monitors on a defined schedule, not just at commissioning — LIM calibration drifts over time.
nfpa_check_4: Confirm essential electrical system branches (life safety, critical, equipment) are properly segregated and backed by UPS or generator as required.
nfpa_check_5: Keep documentation of testing and maintenance — accreditation reviews and insurance audits will ask for it.
nfpa_h2_4: Where This Gets Practical for Facility Managers
nfpa_p6: Most compliance gaps we encounter aren't from bad initial design — they're from maintenance drift. A line isolation monitor that's never recalibrated, a distribution board that was modified without updating documentation, or an operating room repurposed from a lower-risk space without a corresponding electrical upgrade. Building to NFPA 99 once isn't enough; it needs a maintenance program behind it.

ipp_blog_post_title: Why Your Hospital Needs Isolated Power Panels
ipp_blog_excerpt: The risk isolated power panels solve in operating rooms, how they work, and when NFPA 99 requires one.
ipp_blog_h1: Why Your Hospital Needs Isolated Power Panels
ipp_blog_subhead: The risk they solve, how they work, and when NFPA 99 requires one
ipp_blog_p1: Ask most hospital administrators what keeps them up at night about facility infrastructure, and power reliability is near the top. But there's a more specific risk that's easy to overlook until you understand it: what happens if a single ground fault occurs in an operating room mid-procedure?
ipp_blog_h2_1: The Problem Ordinary Electrical Systems Have in Operating Rooms
ipp_blog_p2: In a standard grounded electrical system, a ground fault — current unintentionally finding a path to ground — trips a breaker to protect people and equipment. That's the correct behavior almost everywhere in a building. But in an operating room, where a patient and surgical equipment can form part of that path through conductive fluids, an abrupt power cut mid-procedure isn't a safety feature. It's a new hazard.
ipp_blog_p3: This is precisely the scenario isolated power systems are designed to prevent.
ipp_blog_h2_2: How an Isolated Power Panel Actually Works
ipp_blog_p4: An isolated power panel (IPP) uses an isolation transformer to separate the operating room's electrical circuit from the building's grounded system. Neither conductor is directly referenced to ground, so a single fault doesn't create the low-resistance path needed to trip a breaker or interrupt power.
ipp_blog_p5: Instead, a line isolation monitor (LIM) continuously watches both conductors for a developing fault and sounds an alarm the moment one occurs — typically well before it becomes dangerous. The surgical team gets a clear signal that something needs attention, without power being interrupted mid-procedure. The fault is usually corrected between procedures rather than during one.
ipp_blog_h2_3: When Is an IPP Actually Required?
ipp_blog_p6: NFPA 99 requires isolated power systems for "wet procedure locations" — spaces where a patient is likely to come into contact with both electrical equipment and conductive liquid at the same time. In practice, this typically covers:
ipp_blog_scenario_3: Certain critical care and intensive care areas, per facility risk assessment
ipp_blog_scenario_4: Some obstetric delivery rooms, depending on procedure type
ipp_blog_p7: The exact classification depends on your facility's risk assessment and design consultant's determination — not every patient care space needs one, but the spaces that do need one absolutely cannot substitute a standard grounded system instead.
ipp_blog_h2_4: What This Means If You're Planning or Renovating a Facility
ipp_blog_p8: If you're building a new operating suite, converting a space to a higher-risk use, or simply inheriting a facility where you're not confident the existing electrical infrastructure matches current code, the isolated power system is not an area to guess on. It requires equipment properly rated for the application (transformer, line isolation monitor, and branch circuit breakers matched to the panel), correct installation and equipotential grounding, and ongoing testing — a LIM that drifts out of calibration defeats the purpose of having one.

cs_ipp_h1: Isolated Power for a Hospital Operating Theatre Suite
cs_ipp_sub: Bringing a multi-theatre surgical suite in the Eastern Province in line with NFPA 99
cs_ipp_c1: A private hospital in the Eastern Province was expanding its surgical capacity and needed the new operating theatres to satisfy NFPA 99 requirements for wet procedure locations. Their design consultant had classified the theatres as Category 1 spaces, which meant isolated power was required rather than optional.
cs_ipp_c2: The complication was not the new build. It was that several existing theatres in the adjoining wing had been commissioned years earlier, and their line isolation monitors had never been recalibrated. Any accreditation review would have looked at the suite as a whole.
cs_ipp_w1: We began with a survey of the existing suite rather than quoting only the new theatres, so the hospital could see the whole compliance picture before committing to a scope.
cs_ipp_w2: For the new theatres we supplied and installed isolated power panels with integrated line isolation monitors, each feeding a dedicated reference-grounding point and the theatre’s critical branch outlets. Panels were selected for compatibility with the Bender and PG LifeLink equipment already used elsewhere in the facility, so the biomedical team would not be maintaining two different families of hardware.
cs_ipp_w3: For the existing theatres we recalibrated the monitors, corrected documentation that no longer matched the installed distribution, and handed over a testing schedule.
cs_ipp_w4: Installation and commissioning were sequenced around the theatre schedule, working in the gaps between surgical lists rather than requiring the suite to close.
cs_ipp_o1: The new theatres were commissioned with isolated power systems and line isolation monitoring in place, and the existing theatres were brought back to a documented, tested state.
cs_ipp_o2: The hospital now holds a single maintenance schedule covering every theatre in the suite. In our experience the majority of NFPA 99 gaps are not design failures but maintenance drift, so the schedule matters as much as the hardware.
cs_ev_h1: EV Charging Rollout Across a Commercial Retail Complex
cs_ev_sub: AC and DC charging for a mixed retail and office development, sized for growth
cs_ev_c1: The operator of a mixed retail and office development wanted EV charging in its parking structure. The commercial driver was tenant demand and Vision 2030 alignment; the constraint was the existing electrical infrastructure.
cs_ev_c2: The initial request was for a large number of fast chargers. An early load assessment showed the incoming supply could not support that without a substation upgrade that would have dominated the budget.
cs_ev_w1: We started with an electrical capacity assessment rather than a charger quotation, because the answer to "how many chargers" is determined by the supply, not by the parking count.
cs_ev_w2: The deployment we recommended mixed a small number of DC fast chargers near the retail entrance, where dwell time is short and speed matters, with a larger number of AC Level 2 units in the office parking area, where vehicles sit for hours and slower charging is sufficient. This served more vehicles per riyal of electrical capacity than an all-DC design.
cs_ev_w3: All units were specified as OCPP-compliant so the operator is not locked to a single vendor’s management platform, and integrated with a payment system so charging could be billed rather than absorbed as a service cost.
cs_ev_w4: Containment and distribution were sized for a second phase, so adding units later means pulling cable, not revisiting the switchgear.
cs_ev_o1: The complex went live with a working mix of AC and DC charging within the existing electrical supply, avoiding the substation upgrade the original brief would have required.
cs_ev_o2: Because the distribution was sized ahead of demand, the operator can expand as EV uptake grows without repeating the civil works.
cs_ups_h1: UPS Replacement on a Healthcare Critical Branch
cs_ups_sub: Replacing end-of-life power backup in a live facility, without a shutdown window
cs_ups_c1: A healthcare facility was running UPS units that had passed end of life. Batteries were no longer holding their rated autonomy, and replacement parts for the units themselves were becoming difficult to source.
cs_ups_c2: The units protected the critical branch feeding patient monitoring and diagnostic equipment. There was no acceptable shutdown window: the equipment they protected could not simply be switched off while the UPS was swapped.
cs_ups_w1: We specified online double-conversion units, which suit this load type because they isolate connected equipment from mains disturbances continuously rather than switching over on failure.
cs_ups_w2: Sizing was based on a measured load survey rather than the nameplate rating of the outgoing units. Critical branches accumulate equipment over years, and the real load rarely matches what was installed against originally.
cs_ups_w3: The changeover was carried out through a temporary bypass arrangement so the protected load stayed energised throughout. Each unit was transferred, commissioned and load-tested before the next was started.
cs_ups_w4: We handed over a battery replacement schedule with the system, since batteries, not electronics, are what typically end a UPS installation’s useful life.
cs_ups_o1: The critical branch is protected by current-generation equipment with full rated autonomy restored and a supported spare parts path.
cs_ups_o2: Clinical operations continued throughout the replacement. No shutdown window was required.
cs_light_h1: Obstruction and Helipad Lighting for a High-Rise Development
cs_light_sub: Aviation warning lighting and rooftop helipad lighting on a tall building
cs_light_c1: A high-rise development required aviation obstruction lighting to mark the structure, plus lighting for a rooftop helipad intended for emergency medical access.
cs_light_c2: Aviation lighting is unlike architectural lighting: the specification is driven by aviation authority requirements for intensity, colour, flash characteristics and failure monitoring, not by aesthetics. A fitting that merely looks correct is not compliant.
cs_light_w1: We specified obstruction lighting to the intensity class appropriate to the structure’s height, with the fixture layout set by the building’s profile so the outline is marked correctly from every approach angle.
cs_light_w2: For the helipad we installed perimeter lighting, the touchdown and lift-off area marking, and an illuminated windsock, with the layout following the approved helipad geometry.
cs_light_w3: Both systems were connected to a monitored control panel so a failed fixture raises an alarm rather than being discovered at the next inspection. On an obstruction lighting system, silent failure is the actual risk.
cs_light_w4: Circuits were backed so that a loss of normal supply does not extinguish the obstruction lighting.
cs_light_o1: The structure is marked in line with aviation requirements, and the helipad is lit for night operations.
cs_light_o2: Because failures are monitored and alarmed, the facilities team learns about a failed fixture when it happens rather than at an inspection.
cs_hvac_h1: HVAC Upgrade for a Hospitality Property
cs_hvac_sub: Improving guest comfort and control in an operating hotel, floor by floor
cs_hvac_c1: An operating hotel was receiving recurring guest complaints about inconsistent room temperatures. Some floors ran cold while others could not hold setpoint during the afternoon peak.
cs_hvac_c2: The property could not take a wing out of service for a full replacement, and the plant had to keep running through a Saudi summer while the work was carried out.
cs_hvac_w1: We surveyed the existing distribution before proposing equipment. The imbalance turned out to be substantially a distribution and control problem rather than a shortfall of installed capacity, which changed the shape of the project considerably.
cs_hvac_w2: Air handling units were refurbished or replaced where condition justified it, ductwork was rebalanced, and zone controls were brought back to a state where a setpoint in a room actually governed that room.
cs_hvac_w3: Controls were integrated with the building management system so the engineering team can see performance per zone instead of responding to individual guest complaints.
cs_hvac_w4: The work was phased floor by floor, with each floor returned to service before the next was started, so the property never lost more than a single floor’s inventory at a time.
cs_hvac_o1: Room temperatures hold setpoint consistently across floors, including through the afternoon peak.
cs_hvac_o2: The engineering team now has per-zone visibility through the BMS, which turns comfort management from a reactive task into a monitored one.
cs_hvac_o3: The property remained open and trading throughout, losing only one floor of inventory at any given time.
pp_sub: How Black Arrow Venture collects, uses and protects your information.
pp_intro: Black Arrow Venture company (“Black Arrow”, “we”, “us”) operates www.blackarrowksa.com. This policy explains what personal data we collect through this website, why we collect it, and what you can do about it.
pp_collect_lead: We only collect what you choose to send us. Specifically:
pp_collect_list:
• Contact and partnership enquiries — your name, company name, email address, phone number, the service you selected, and the content of your message.
  • Newsletter signup — your email address.
  • Language preference — stored in your browser only (see Cookies below).
pp_no_trackers: We do not run advertising trackers, and we do not buy or sell contact lists.
pp_why: Enquiry data is used solely to respond to your enquiry, prepare quotations, and carry out any resulting commercial relationship. Newsletter addresses are used only to send occasional company and product updates, and every message includes an unsubscribe option.
pp_who_lead: Two service providers necessarily handle data on our behalf:
pp_who_list:
• Web3Forms — receives form submissions and forwards them to our email.
  • Vercel — hosts this website and processes standard server logs, including IP addresses, for security and reliability.
pp_no_share: We do not share your information with anyone else except where required by Saudi law.
pp_cookies: This site sets no advertising or analytics cookies. We store a single value in your browser’s local storage — your language preference (English or Arabic) — so the site opens in the language you chose. You can clear it at any time through your browser settings.
pp_retention: Enquiry correspondence is retained for as long as needed to serve you and to meet our commercial and tax record-keeping obligations, then deleted. Newsletter addresses are kept until you unsubscribe.
pp_rights: Under the Saudi Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL) you may request access to the personal data we hold about you, ask us to correct it, ask us to delete it, or withdraw consent to marketing contact. Email info@blackarrowksa.com and we will respond within 30 days.
pp_security: This site is served over HTTPS with HSTS enforced. Enquiry data is transmitted over encrypted connections. No system is perfectly secure, but we take reasonable technical and organisational measures to protect your information.
pp_changes: If we change this policy we will update the date at the top of this page.
